records.title: Late Victorian or Edwardian, c.1880–1910: Glazed breakfront display cabinet, dining room (furniture seen in photographs of Great House Farm)

date.display: Late Victorian or Edwardian, c.1880–1910 (judged from photographs; not checked)

records.place_text: Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough — Dining room
records.description: Display cabinet / bookcase. Room: Dining room. Visible features: Three-bay glazed upper section over a closed base; carved cresting with finials along the top; projecting centre (breakfront); used to display china and glass. Dating basis: Glazed upper doors with astragal glazing bars, carved cresting with turned finials and a projecting centre section are typical of late nineteenth-century cabinet work; judged from the photographs only. Seen in 3 photograph(s) of the Great House Farm photograph set, Part 1. Identified from the photographs only; the object has not been examined.

records.title: 14 Sep 1995: The Post (Cardiff), p.24, “My Cardiff” column, “The day that the radio age was born” (Marconi and George Kemp at Great House Farm, night of 10–11 May 1897)

date.display: 14 September 1995

records.place_text: Great House Farm, Llandough; Lavernock Point
records.description: Published local-history column by Bill Barrett in The Post (Cardiff), 14 September 1995, page 24. The column describes Guglielmo Marconi and George Kemp calling at Great House Farm, Llandough, close to midnight on the eve of 11 May 1897 to hire the farmer’s horse and trap to carry apparatus to Lavernock Point. It opens with the Rotary Club of Cardiff plaque at St Lawrence Church, Lavernock. A photograph on the page shows Cardiff Post Office engineers with the Marconi equipment on Lavernock Point. The column was written 98 years after the events it describes.
records.transcript_status: Copy of the printed page held; transcript on the former research page.

provenance.obtained: Moved from the former research page /research/evidence/ev-0646-the-post-cardiff-1995-09-14-p24-marconi-great-house-farm/ on 11 November 2026; copy of the printed page held.

scope.label: In scope: press item naming Great House Farm
scope.reason: Names Great House Farm in an account of the May 1897 wireless experiments.

records.title: 1849: Samuel Lewis, A Topographical Dictionary of Wales, parish entry “Llandough (Llan-Dôch), or Llan-Doche-Penarth”

date.display: 1849 (published)

records.place_text: Llandough-juxta-Penarth parish
records.description: Printed gazetteer entry for the parish of Llandough in the poor-law union of Cardiff, hundred of Dinas Powys: 4 miles south-west of Cardiff, 133 inhabitants, a discharged rectory united with Leckwith and Cogan. The entry records a tradition of a fifth-century monastery and notes that it is not supported by any satisfactory authority. It also describes the church dedicated to Dochdwy with the shaft of an old circular cross, a school, Cogan Pill, a small circular mound south-east of the church, the marshes, the limestone and the view over the Ely and Taff. Read in a public transcription; the printed volume has not been seen and the exact printed page within pp. 524–536 is not marked.
records.transcript_status: Public transcription read; printed volume not seen.

records.title: Year 1886 inscribed: photograph of a “John Williams / 1886” inscription, kept as a handwriting comparator for the 1939 tenancy agreement signature

date.display: inscription bears the year 1886; when it was written is not established

records.place_text: not disclosed
records.description: Photograph of an inscription reading “John Williams” with the year “1886”, supplied by a family member on 30 October 2026. It is kept beside the 1939 tenancy agreement (EV-0023) as a visual comparator for the tenant signature. Surface observations only: the inscription has an ornate capital J, wide letter spacing and an extended final stroke; the 1939 signature is more compact. Not authenticated. Who wrote the inscription, when, whether the year was written at the same time, the identity and location of the object, and whether it relates to the same John Williams are not known. A visible difference between a display inscription and a signature does not establish different writers.
